doc.title: Bill Kirchner interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 4, 2021

title: Emotion versus theory in improvisation
summary: Kirchner says improvisation needs both emotion and knowledge, instinctual or theoretical, citing Chet Baker's ears.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: For me it begs the question, sometimes you read comments about jazz and I think they’re usually written, not the musician writers, the non-musician writers, who say jazz musicians play what they feel. And I’ve had this debate with myself about how much emotion is connected to improvisation. Is it driven by emotion and feeling or is it driven by more theoretical knowledge? I know what chord I’m playing here and I know that this will sound out, this will sound in. I’m not sure that’s a question but it’s — I’ll let you try to deal with it.

Yeah I probably, my answer would be it’s all of the above. I mean certainly emotion should have an important bearing on it because if it isn’t then why are we doing it? But also I mean you have to have a solid either theoretical knowledge or some kind of instinctual thing about the music. I mean somebody, there are some great players like for example Chet Baker knew nothing about harmony in a theoretical sense but he had great ears. So you know I mean he had his own kind of knowledge. You know it was an instinctual thing and it wasn’t based on music theory but it was knowledge nonetheless. So you know if you have the instinctual knowledge or the theoretical knowledge of some sort combined with the emotional thing, that that’s where substantial music comes from I would think. That’s been my experience anyway.
